prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a neighbour's house flooded last winter. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a neighbour’s property has flooded, I should separate the cause of damage from the location of the affected items, because water can travel between homes and the insured peril may still be clear even if the source was next door."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the incident followed prolonged winter rainfall, I should check whether the loss ties to surface water, overflowing drains, or river flooding, as the wording and delegated decisions can differ depending on the route of water ingress."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a claimant reports damp or staining rather than obvious standing water, I should treat it as potentially linked to a prior flood event and ask for timeline details, because hidden saturation often shows up later than the main incident."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I have enough evidence that the neighbour’s flood caused sudden and accidental damage, I prefer to progress the claim within authority rather than hold it for unnecessary review, provided there are no signs of maintenance failure or gradual seepage."},{"type":"fact","content":"When internal decoration, flooring, and low-level fittings are affected, I should expect drying and strip-out to be more likely than immediate replacement, and I should distinguish urgent mitigation from final settlement."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a winter flood has affected multiple homes on the same street, I should look for consistent weather and local drainage evidence, because a shared pattern can support the claim without requiring a perfect account from every neighbour."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a policyholder mentions that emergency services or local authorities were involved, I should record it, but I should not assume liability or cover automatically follows from the event being widespread."},{"type":"preference","content":"When photos are available, I prefer images taken in sequence from the source of water through to the damaged rooms, because they help me judge extent, drying needs, and whether the claim remains within delegated authority."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a flooded neighbour’s home led to secondary damage from contaminated water or repeated re-entry of water, I should be alert to increased cleaning and disposal costs, since those cases usually need a more careful reserve estimate."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the claimant worries mainly about future flood risk rather than current damage, I should acknowledge that concern but keep the triage focused on present loss, because worry alone does not change the assessment of the current claim."}]}
